name: Mamusi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wade, Aaron. 2016-2021 (ms. printed 2022-09-13). Organised Phonology Data: Mamusi Language [KDF]. Ukarumpa: SIL. 7 pp. Draft, posted as-is without peer review. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 92954 (replaces a 2017 version).
catalog_quote: Stress is apparently non-phonemic and predictable. In general, stress occurs on the penultimate syllable, unless the ultimate syllable is closed (almost always with /ŋ/), in which case stress is attracted to the ultimate. No minimal pairs have been discovered differing only in stress placement. Vowel lengthening occurs predictably with stress and is non-phonemic. There may be conrasting consonant length, but it has only been observed in morphologically conditioned settings. For example, sonorants may be lengthened or geminated to indicate IMPERFECTIVE aspect as in [u.tu.'mɑ.lɑ] ‘arrive’ vs. [u.tu.'mɑl.lɑ] ‘arrive.IPFV’. This is analyzed as a form of reduplication (the normal pattern is [CV]) and is not considered phonemic.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Page 4, section headed 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', reads exactly: 'Stress is apparently non-phonemic and predictable. In general, stress occurs on the penultimate syllable, unless the ultimate syllable is closed (almost always with /ŋ/), in which case stress is attracted to the ultimate. (only difference is a line-break hyphen in 'non-/phonemic'). The section continues with morphologically conditioned sonorant gemination for IMP…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable unless the final syllable is closed (in practice almost always by /ŋ/, the only regular word-final consonant), in which case the final syllable is stressed. Stress is non-contrastive; stressed vowels are lengthened. Transcriptions in the same document confirm: [le.ˈsi.nɑ] 'four', [ɔu.lɔ.ˈŋɑ.nɑ] 'middle' (penult) vs. [lim.ˈpuŋ] 'flooring wood', [mɔ.tɔ.ˈniŋ] 'chair', [u.ˈweŋ] 'mosquito' (final). A closed penult does not attract stress away from the default ([u.tu.'mɑl.lɑ] 'arrive.IPFV').
new_statements.exceptions: Two words with non-nasal final consonants, marked as likely borrowings, keep penultimate stress ([kɑ.ˈlɑ.ŋɑr] 'parakeet', [ˈka.lis] 'bandicoot'); the rule is phrased 'in general' and 'apparently', and the document is a draft based on the author's five years in the language.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a phonemic wordlist; no phrase-level discussion. Data are from the Mamusi language generally (major villages Sivauna, Auna, Kaitoto, Kinsena, Bili); the only dialect named is the central (Masapa) dialect, in a footnote about loss of initial /ŋ/.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD is titled for the Mamusi language [kdf] as a whole (Glottolog mamu1254; ISO kdf), located in West Pomio District, East New Britain; it names the central (Masapa) dialect only in a footnote on initial /ŋ/ loss and gives no data labelled Kakuna/Melkoi (the western dialect; Ross 1988 and Chowning 1969 treat Kakuna as a dialect of Mamusi). No separate glottocode for the dialects.

sources.note: p. 4 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': stress non-phonemic and predictable; penultimate by default, but a closed final syllable (almost always closed by /ŋ/) attracts stress to the ultima; no minimal pairs; vowel length is a predictable concomitant of stress. Transcribed examples pp. 1-4 agree ([le.ˈsi.nɑ], [ɔu.lɔ.ˈŋɑ.nɑ] vs. [lim.ˈpuŋ], [mɔ.tɔ.ˈniŋ]); two likely loans with non-nasal codas keep penult stress ([kɑ.ˈlɑ.ŋɑr], [ˈka.lis]). Nothing on secondary stress.
